notes.1a: Candidates did not perform well on this question. Most candidates were unable to provide an appropriate explanation although invariably they were able to apply their knowledge in part (b).
notes.1b: This was well answered by most candidates. The most common errors included the incorrect treatment of carriage inwards and direct expenses and also posting the factory machinery depreciation incorrectly.
notes.1c: Most candidates made the transfer from the manufacturing account correctly and computed the gross profit. Few, however, were able to correctly calculate the values of the opening and closing inventories.
notes.1d: This was not answered well with few candidates accounting for the unrealised profit.
notes.1e: This was well answered with most candidates giving a decision and then justifying it with appropriate reasoning.
notes.2b: The income statement was well prepared. Some candidates made errors in adjusting the shop purchases. A few candidates also included expenses not related to the shop.
notes.2c: The income and expenditure account was also prepared to an acceptable standard. Some candidates incorrectly calculated subscriptions and many did not adjust the rent of catering facilities correctly.
notes.2d: This was well answered although errors often occurred in posting the subscriptions in arrears and subscriptions in advance.
notes.2e: Though most candidates provided a decision and a reasoned justification, responses were often repetitive.
notes.3a: This was very well answered with most candidates stating two correct advantages.
notes.3b: Again, well answered with most calculating the ratios correctly. The most common error was not accounting for the preference shares dividend.
notes.3c: The ratio calculations proved to be more testing with many not being able to adjust the given data correctly.
notes.3i: There was some reasonable analysis but many candidates mixed up the two years and treated year ending 31 December 2016 as year ending 31 December 2015 and vice versa.
notes.3ii: Most candidates provided reasonable advice to justify their decision including the implication of the intended issue of the debentures.
notes.4a: Most candidates were able to state the meaning of ‘capital account’.
notes.4b: The preparation of the sole trader capital accounts was not well answered with only a few candidates correctly accounting for the profit or loss on revaluation or making the correct cash
notes.4c: The partnership capital accounts were prepared to a higher standard with many candidates scoring full marks by bringing forward their sole trader balances and making correct cash adjustment.
notes.4d: This was well answered although many did not enter the cash and cash equivalents correctly.
notes.4e: Most candidates correctly identified that one partner was better off and one was worse off based on profitability but did not consider other relevant matters.
notes.4f: Most candidates correctly identified two advantages. Since this was a ‘discuss’ question candidates should have developed their identified advantage to obtain full credit.
notes.5a: There were weak responses to this question with many just identifying ‘discounts due to bulk
notes.5b: This was well answered with many correctly calculating total profit and profit per unit together with the decrease.
notes.5c: The calculation of the variances was not well answered with relatively few calculating all correctly.
notes.5d: Responses were weak with few appropriate explanations.
notes.5e: Most candidates obtained two of the three available marks by giving the required advice and justifying it by the change in profit.
notes.6a: This was well answered with most candidates making the correct apportionment.
notes.6b: Most were able to then calculate the profit or loss per unit. A few candidates worked in totals and could not convert to a unitary value as required.
notes.6c: Most candidates were able to apply the accountant’s analysis but there were relatively few fully correct solutions. The most common error was not being able to apportion the remaining overheads on the basis of sales units.
notes.6d: This was well answered with most candidates making a correct calculation based on their own brought forward figures.
notes.6e: Most candidates gave a decision but the justification was invariably generic and did not consider the products.
notes.6f: Responses were acceptable with most being able to state the required meanings of the given ACCOUNTING
notes.key_messages: Candidates need to understand the link between entries in the journals and the posting of them to the relevant ledger accounts and also movement of funds between accounts with in the same section of the statement of financial position. General comments A number of questions proved straightforward and were well attempted: 1, 3, 5, 6, 8, 14 and 16. notes.general_comments: General comments A number of questions proved straightforward and were well attempted: 1, 3, 5, 6, 8, 14 and 16. There was only one question where less than 30 per cent of candidates identified the correct key. This and some other questions have been here. Comments on specific questions The most common response was that the error would only be revealed when Henry prepared a purchases ledger control account. From the given data Henry reversed the entry, but did enter the correct amount in the purchases journal. This would mean that he also posted a debit and credit of equal amount in the ledger.
